info.description: An API which allows to retrieve data about the **Roman Calendar** for any given year, between 1970 and 9999. The data strives for historical accuracy (memorials and feast days are only generated from the year in which they were effectively introduced). The data is based on original sources (Roman Missals, Decrees of the Dicastery for Divine Worship and the Discipline of the Sacraments, Mysterii Paschalis, etc.), not on data copied or retrieved from online sources which may not be accurate. The API offers multiple locales and multiple calendars, from the **General Roman Calendar** to national or diocesan calendars. The Roman rite is the default and may also be requested explicitly with a `/calendar/roman` prefix (equivalent to no prefix); a `/calendar/ambrosian` prefix selects the Ambrosian rite, available from 1976 onward. The Ambrosian rite has no national calendars: its dioceses (Milano, Bergamo, Novara, Lugano) are layered directly on the comune ambrosiano.

get.summary: Retrieve liturgical events for the Ambrosian calendar (comune ambrosiano) for each day of the current year
get.description: Retrieves liturgical events for the Ambrosian rite (comune ambrosiano only; no diocesan overlay) for each day of the current year. There is no national layer for the Ambrosian rite. The epiphany, ascension, and corpus_christi query parameters are accepted for consistency with the Roman rite endpoints but are IGNORED under the Ambrosian rite: Epiphany is fixed to January 6th, Ascension to the 40th day after Easter (Thursday), and Corpus Christi to its rite-fixed placement. The values actually applied are announced ahead of any request at `ambrosian_calendars[].settings` on `/calendars`, and the response `settings` block echoes those rite-fixed values rather than whatever was requested. Readings are currently an empty placeholder (no Ambrosian lectionary yet); year cycles, first-vespers vigils, and psalter-week numbering are provisional pending ordo validation. The Ambrosian rite has liturgical books only in Italian and Latin, as declared by `ambrosian_calendars[].locales` on `/calendars`: a `locale` parameter naming any other language returns 400 Bad Request, while an `Accept-Language` header asking for one is negotiated against that set (falling back to Latin) rather than rejected.

post.summary: Authenticate user and obtain JWT tokens
post.description: Authenticate with username and password to obtain access and refresh tokens. Tokens are returned in the response body AND set as HttpOnly cookies (litcal_access_token, litcal_refresh_token). Browser clients should use the cookie-based authentication (preferred for XSS protection), while server-to-server clients can use the Bearer token in the Authorization header.

200.description: OK: Authentication successful. Tokens returned in response body and set as HttpOnly cookies.

post.summary: Refresh access token using refresh token
post.description:
Use a valid refresh token to obtain a new access token without re-authenticating with username/password.

**Token Sources (in order of precedence):**
1. **HttpOnly Cookie** (preferred): The refresh token is automatically read from the `litcal_refresh_token` cookie if present. Browser-based clients using cookie authentication can call this endpoint without a request body.
2. **Request Body** (fallback): If no cookie is present, the refresh token must be provided in the JSON request body.

**Usage:**
- **Browser clients**: Use `credentials: 'include'` in fetch requests. No request body needed if cookies were set by `/auth/login`.
- **Server/API clients**: Send the refresh token in the request body.

requestBody.description: Optional when using cookie-based authentication. Required for clients that don't send cookies.

Approve every still-`submitted` row in the batch. Requires the `admin` relation on the batch's resource (global admins bypass the OpenFGA check). Returns 404, never 403, when the caller does not administer the batch's resource — identical to an unknown batch id, so a 403 cannot confirm to the caller that a batch they cannot touch exists at all. Returns 409 if the batch was already approved, rejected, or withdrawn by someone else before this request landed.

Before anything is transitioned, every still-`submitted` row is re-validated against the JSON schema that governs its path **at this moment**, not the one in force when it was submitted. If any row no longer validates the approval is refused with 422, the batch is left untouched (still `submitted`, every row intact), and the `detail` names each offending file, the schema that refused it, and the violation. Rows carrying no content — a delete — have nothing to validate and are skipped. There is no override: the submitter must withdraw and re-submit against the current schema, or the batch must be rejected (rejection is deliberately not gated on validation). Approving records the decision; publication is the publisher's separate step, tracked by `publication_status` — see the change-request runbook.

post.summary: Promote a locale to officially supported
post.description:
Adds the locale to `general_roman_calendar.official` in jsondata/supportedLocales.json, through the same write seam every other source-data edit uses: a reviewable change request where SOURCEDATA_CHANGE_REQUESTS is configured, a direct disk write where it is not. See the `curation` object of GET /admin/locales for which of the two this deployment will do.

Takes no request body.

Gated on the readiness probes of GET /admin/locales/{locale}, and the gate is NOT bypassable — there is no force parameter and no role that skips it. Promotion is not a label: an official locale is served strictly, so `ReadingsMap::getReadings()` throws on a missing readings entry instead of degrading quietly. Promoting an unready locale therefore converts silent gaps into 500s on a calendar the API advertises as supported.

A promotion also drops the locale's note from `candidates`, whose prose says why it was not yet official and is false once it is.

Restricted to global admins. Holding `admin` on `rite_calendar:roman/supported_locales` does not open the endpoint; it decides whether the resulting change request is auto-approved or waits for a reviewer. Unlike the write routes guarded by the authorization middleware, this auto-approval check carries NO legacy `general_roman_calendar:supported_locales` fallback: during the #955 migration window a caller holding only the deprecated tuple has their change request queued for a reviewer rather than auto-approved, which resumes once the tuple migration has run.

parameters.description: The locale to promote. Must be one of the candidates returned by GET /admin/locales.

200.description: OK

post.summary: Demote a locale from officially supported
post.description:
Removes the locale from `general_roman_calendar.official` in jsondata/supportedLocales.json, through the same write seam as the promotion above. Takes no request body.

Deliberately NOT readiness-gated, and the asymmetry is the point: demotion LOOSENS enforcement, so the same missing readings that would have thrown now degrade quietly, and it can never turn a working calendar into a 500. What it can do is change published output silently — /calendars stops advertising the locale, and affected events serve nothing instead of erroring — which is a governance risk answered by review and the audit trail, not by a readiness probe.

Two integrity guards still apply, both 409: the locale must currently be official, and the LAST official locale may not be removed. An empty `official` list is indistinguishable from an unreadable resource, so the API would silently fall back to its built-in list rather than supporting nothing.

get.summary: Retrieve an Ambrosian diocesan calendar data resource
get.description:
Retrieve the source definition of a diocesan calendar defined under the Ambrosian rite.

**The `ambrosian` rite segment is required here, not decorative.** The bare `/data/diocese/{key}` form resolves to the Roman rite, so addressing an Ambrosian diocese through it returns `422 Unprocessable Content` (`Diocesan calendar ... belongs to the ambrosian rite, not the requested roman rite.`); the same `422` is returned on this path for a diocese that is not Ambrosian. The Ambrosian dioceses are Milano (`milano_it`), Bergamo (`bergam_it`), Novara (`novara_it`) and Lugano (`lugano_ch`) — every other diocese is Roman. On any `/data` path `roman` is accepted as an explicit synonym of the bare form.

Only the diocesan tier exists under more than one rite, so there is deliberately no `/data/ambrosian/nation/{key}` and no `/data/ambrosian/widerregion/{key}`: the Ambrosian rite is proper to the Archdiocese of Milan and a handful of neighbouring dioceses rather than to any nation or region, and the source tree has no Ambrosian national or wider-region partition to read or write. Either of those requests returns `400 Bad Request`.

Unlike `/calendar` and `/events`, `/data` advertises no canonical URL: the bare form returns no RFC 6596 `Link: <...>; rel="canonical"` response header.

The Ambrosian rite has approved liturgical books only in Italian and Latin, so `diocesan_calendars[].locales` on `/calendars` declares `it_IT` and `la_VA` for these dioceses; a `locale` naming any other language returns `422 Unprocessable Content`.

get.summary: Retrieve the stored translations of a national calendar
get.description:
Retrieve the stored translations of a national calendar's own liturgical events, as a map of `event_key` to translated name. This is a different resource from `/data/nation/{key}`, which the path hangs off: that returns the calendar definition, this returns the translation file behind it.

Only `GET` and `POST` exist at this depth. `RegionalDataHandler::validateRequestPath()` accepts two or three path segments for those two methods and exactly two for the others, and the router narrows the allowed methods to `GET` and `POST` for any three-segment `/data` path, so a `PUT`, `PATCH` or `DELETE` carrying a third segment is refused with `400 Bad Request` (`Expected two path params for PUT, PATCH and DELETE requests, received 3`). `POST` is a read alias of `GET`.

The third segment binds to `i18nRequest`. It is not the `locale` parameter that `/data/nation/{key}` accepts, and the two are documented separately for that reason.

An unknown nation is refused with `422 Unprocessable Content`; a nation that exists but has no translation file for the requested locale gives `404 Not Found`. `/data/roman/nation/{key}/{i18n_locale}` states the same rite explicitly and is the canonical form of this path.

**Deprecated in favour of the explicit-rite form `/data/roman/nation/{key}/{i18n_locale}`,** which is canonical. This path keeps working unchanged and returns an identical response — it is deliberately not redirected, because these routes accept POST and a redirect would both downgrade POST to GET and break preflighted cross-origin requests. put.summary: Create a new unit test at its own URI in the API `tests` folder
put.description: Create (`PUT`) requires the `editor` relation. When fine-grained authorization (OpenFGA) is enabled, the request body must be JSON: the authorization scope is resolved from the parsed JSON payload's `applies_to`, so YAML or form-encoded bodies fail closed with a 403. The `{rite}` path segment and the body's `applies_to.rite` must name the same rite, or the request is rejected with a 422. The body may optionally echo the `scope` the API previously returned: a `scope` that matches the server-resolved value is accepted and silently stripped before persisting; a `scope` that disagrees is rejected with a 422. `scope` is never required, and is never present in a source file.

patch.summary: Update an existing unit test in the API `tests` folder
patch.description: The `{rite}` path segment and the body's `applies_to.rite` must name the same rite, or the request is rejected with a 422. The body may optionally echo the `scope` the API previously returned: a `scope` that matches the server-resolved value is accepted and silently stripped before persisting; a `scope` that disagrees is rejected with a 422. On `PATCH`, the server-resolved value is always the scope this request's own `applies_to` resolves to — the scope the test WILL have once this write is applied — never the scope it had beforehand; a `PATCH` that changes `applies_to` and echoes the newly-correct scope is accepted, while echoing the now-superseded stored scope is rejected as a mismatch. A `PATCH` that changes `applies_to` (re-scoping the test) additionally requires the `editor` relation on BOTH the scope the test is currently stored under and the scope named by the new `applies_to`; holding `editor` on only one of the two is rejected with a 403, even though the stored-scope check alone would otherwise pass. `scope` is never required, and is never present in a source file.

get.summary: Retrieve the source data this API can be asked to validate
get.description: Clients iterate this list and send back an item's opaque id, so no filesystem path crosses the wire. Advertising is not verification: an item appearing here does not assert that the underlying data is present, only that it is checkable. Filtering by rite and region is done by the client. Each item's `steps` values are the same vocabulary the Health WebSocket protocol's response frames carry in their own `step` field (issue #819, closed); a client should read that field on each frame rather than count them, and stop watching a check on the frame whose `step` is `complete` rather than on reaching `steps.length` -- see the property description on `steps` in LitCalValidationsPath.json. Every arm now emits one frame per published step, so `steps.length` is a reliable count to render one card per step against (issues #821 and #822); it is still not what to wait on, because `complete` stays correct for an arm a later change makes shorter. Pair the stopping rule with a timeout: every request that starts work terminates, with a known hole while issue #823 is open -- a throw inside a promise fulfilment handler skips the terminal frame, and a queued request dropped when a run is superseded is discarded without one. The `complete` frame is sent only in reply to a request that carried a `requestId`, since a new frame (unlike a new field) would make a frame-counting v1 client miscount; a client that stops on `complete` must send a `requestId` on every request.

A general association with liturgical terminology would be as follows * 0 = WEEKDAY * 1 = COMMEMORATION * 2 = OPTIONAL MEMORIAL * 3 = MEMORIAL * 4 = FEAST * 5 = FEAST OF THE LORD * 6 = SOLEMNITY * 7 = event that has precedence over a solemnity However this association is not suitable for displaying the actual *grade* (or *rank*) of the liturgical event in liturgical terms, because some events have a logical importance that does not correspond with their portrayed grade, for example "All Souls Day" is called a "Commemoration" and yet it is given the same importance as a solemnity. Thus "All Souls Day" will have a grade of 6, but should be displayed as "Commemoration" rather than as "Solemnity". Permission.description: A permission entry specifying access to a specific resource

object_type.description: OpenFGA object type. `general_roman_calendar` and `general_roman_calendar_test` are deprecated and accepted only until the #955 prune milestone; use `rite_calendar` and `rite_calendar_test`.

object_id.description: Resource identifier. Ids that name a calendar are rite-qualified as `<rite>/<calendarId>` (e.g. `roman/IT`, `ambrosian/lugano_ch`, `roman/Americas`), because a bare calendar id does not identify a calendar; `rite_calendar` ids are rite-qualified the same way (e.g. `roman/temporale`, `ambrosian/EDITIO_TYPICA_2024`). The deprecated `general_roman_calendar` keeps bare ids (e.g. `temporale`) until the #955 prune milestone.

AccessRequest.description: An access request from the requester's perspective. Returned by GET /auth/access-requests (self-list) and used as the row shape inside AccessRequestListResponse. Admin-only review/sync fields (reviewed_by, zitadel_sync_status, zitadel_sync_error) are intentionally absent here — admin-facing endpoints return AccessRequestAdmin instead. `credentials` stays public so the requester sees what they themselves submitted.

review_notes.description: Reviewer-written note left during approve/reject/revoke. Public because rejected requesters need to see why and may use it to resubmit.

AccessRequestAdmin.description: Admin-only view of an access request. Same shape as AccessRequest plus reviewer identity (`reviewed_by`) and Zitadel-sync diagnostics (`zitadel_sync_status`, `zitadel_sync_error`). The common fields are documented on AccessRequest. Duplicated inline (rather than composed via `allOf` over AccessRequest) because `allOf + additionalProperties: false` doesn't compose under Redocly's strict validator — each sub-schema's `additionalProperties` only sees its own properties and rejects the other side's fields.

reviewed_by.description: Admin-only. Zitadel user ID of the admin who actioned the request, or the literal 'system:cascade' for cascade-revokes. Null while the request is still pending.

zitadel_sync_status.description: Admin-only. Tracks whether the role grant/revoke was successfully synced to Zitadel after the DB transaction committed. Null until the first sync attempt.

zitadel_sync_error.description: Admin-only. Error message from the most recent failed Zitadel sync, if any. Cleared on the next successful sync.

CreateAccessRequestBody.description: Request body for submitting a new access request

justification.description: Why the user needs this access

AccessRequestStatusResponse.description: Authenticated user's current access status, returned by GET /auth/access-requests/status. Combines facts about the user's existing roles and any access requests they have on file with a single derived flag (needs_access_request) that drives the new-user onboarding decision.

has_roles.description: True if the user already has at least one role assigned via Zitadel.

current_roles.description: List of role names currently assigned to the user (e.g., "developer", "calendar_editor"). Empty when has_roles is false.

pending_requests.description: Count of the user's access requests with status=pending (waiting for admin review).

approved_requests.description: Count of the user's access requests with status=approved. May be > 0 even when has_roles is false during the brief window between admin approval and Zitadel role sync.

rejected_requests.description: Count of the user's access requests with status=rejected. A rejected request can be resubmitted via POST /auth/access-requests/{id}/resubmit; until then it remains rejected and the user may want to be shown the rejection notes from the most recent request.

needs_access_request.description: Server-derived hint to clients: true if and only if the user is in the initial "no access yet, nothing in flight" state and should be prompted to submit an access request. Computed as `!has_roles && pending_requests === 0 && approved_requests === 0`. Clients should prefer this over recomputing the rule themselves so the API can evolve the criteria (e.g., add cooling-off windows for rejected users) without coordinated client updates.

valid_roles.description: The role names accepted by POST /auth/access-requests as the requested_role. Provided so clients don't hard-code the list.

AccessRequestListResponse.description: Offset-paginated page of access requests returned by GET /auth/access-requests (the requester's own list). Each item is the public AccessRequest shape — admin-only review/sync fields are not present. See AdminAccessRequestListResponse for the /admin/access-requests envelope.

count.description: Number of items in this page. May be less than `limit` on the last page.

total.description: Total matching rows for this user, ignoring limit/offset.

limit.description: Effective limit applied to this page (default 100 if not supplied).

offset.description: Effective offset of the first item in this page (default 0 if not supplied).

has_more.description: True iff `(offset + count) < total`. False on the final page.

AdminAccessRequestListResponse.description: Offset-paginated page of access requests returned by GET /admin/access-requests. Each item is the AccessRequestAdmin shape, which extends AccessRequest with reviewer identity and Zitadel-sync diagnostics. When a resource admin (non-global) calls this endpoint, filterByAdminAccess is applied to each page after fetching: `count` may be smaller than `limit`, and `total` reflects the pre-filter SQL count; `has_more` still reflects the SQL paginator, so clients should page until `has_more` is false even when individual pages come back short.

count.description: Number of items in this page. May be less than `limit` on the last page, or smaller still for resource admins after post-filtering.

total.description: Total matching rows ignoring limit/offset. For resource admins, this is the pre-filter SQL count.

limit.description: Effective limit applied to this page (default 100 if not supplied).

offset.description: Effective offset of the first item in this page (default 0 if not supplied).

has_more.description: True iff more rows are available beyond this page. For global admins, equals `(offset + count) < total`. For non-global admins, reflects the SQL paginator state — `(offset + pre-filter SQL page size) < total` — rather than the post-filter `count`, so the client stops correctly on the final SQL page even when filterByAdminAccess trimmed it.

ChangeRequestDisposition.description:
How a source-data write that reached commit() was handled — always present on every write response from /data/*, /decrees/{decree_id} and /tests/{rite}/{test_name}, in both write modes.

`applied`: this deployment writes source data straight to disk (SOURCEDATA_CHANGE_REQUESTS unset, or set without Postgres and OpenFGA behind it — see GET /health's source_data_writes block). The response body is otherwise byte-identical to what it has always been.

`submitted`: this deployment has SOURCEDATA_CHANGE_REQUESTS enabled and the caller does not administer the resource, so the write was recorded as a change request instead of touching disk. The resource named in the rest of the response body (e.g. `data`, `decree`) describes the PROPOSED content, not the calendar's current content — nothing has changed yet. See `change_request` for the batch id, and GET /auth/change-requests to track it.

`approved`: same as `submitted`, except the caller already administers the resource, so the batch was auto-approved in the same request it was submitted in. This still does not write to disk: Phase 1 has no publisher, so an approved batch sits at `publication_status: none` until the Phase 2 GitHub integration exists. A deployment without SOURCEDATA_CHANGE_REQUESTS never returns `submitted` or `approved` — every write there is `applied`, unchanged from before this feature existed.

ChangeRequestSubmission.description: Present only when the sibling `disposition` is `submitted` or `approved` — identifies the change request batch this write's staged files were recorded under, in place of being written to disk.

batch_id.description: Pass this to GET /auth/change-requests, POST /auth/change-requests/{batchId}/withdraw, or (for a resource admin) POST /admin/change-requests/{batchId}/approve|reject.

review_status.description: Always equal to the sibling `disposition` — repeated here so the batch object is self-describing once separated from the response it was minted in.

auto_approved.description: True exactly when `disposition` is `approved`: the submitter already administers the resource, so the batch was approved in the same request it was created in, rather than waiting for a separate reviewer.

resource.description: The calendar, decrees corpus, or test scope this whole batch belongs to. Every file in `paths` was staged against this one resource.

type.description: `general_roman_calendar` and `general_roman_calendar_test` are deprecated and accepted only until the #955 prune milestone; use `rite_calendar` and `rite_calendar_test`.

id.description: Rite-qualified as `<rite>/<calendarId>` for calendar-naming types (e.g. `roman/US`), for `rite_calendar` ids (e.g. `roman/decrees`, `roman/supported_locales`, `ambrosian/temporale`), and for the `national_calendar_test` and `diocesan_calendar_test` scopes. The deprecated `general_roman_calendar` keeps bare ids such as `decrees` until the #955 prune milestone; `general_roman_calendar_test` also stays bare, as does `rite_calendar_test`, whose id is itself the rite.

paths.description: Repository-relative path of every file staged in this one request (e.g. a diocesan calendar plus its i18n translation files), which is why this can hold more than one entry even though the request targeted a single resource.

superseded_batch_ids.description: Batch ids this submission FOLDED INTO itself; empty when it superseded nothing. Save-equals-submit keeps at most one pending proposal per (file path, submitter), so a write that stages a path you already have pending supersedes the batch that path belonged to. A listed id no longer exists and no longer appears in GET /auth/change-requests — which is why it is reported — but nothing you had pending was discarded: the rows for the paths this request restaged were replaced by it, and every other file that batch held (a superseded batch may have held files this request never mentioned) was carried forward onto the new batch id, so the new batch is your cumulative proposal. For an aggregate file such as decrees.json the edits themselves are preserved too: the new batch was rebuilt from your own pending content.

ChangeRequestBatch.description: One batch of proposed source-data file changes: every row submitted together by a single API write request, collapsed into one object. Returned by GET /admin/change-requests (every batch a caller may review) and GET /auth/change-requests (a caller's own submitted batches). `permissions` is the OpenFGA tuple the server itself checks to decide whether the caller may approve/reject this batch — clients do not need to interpret it, only resource_type/resource_id/review_status/publication_status. The decision and publication columns — `rejected_reason`, `pr_number`, `branch`, `commit_sha`, `merge_commit_sha` and `publication_settled_at` — are returned identically to both audiences: none of them identifies a reviewer, and the rejection reason exists precisely so that the submitter can read it.

resource_type.description: `general_roman_calendar` and `general_roman_calendar_test` are deprecated and accepted only until the #955 prune milestone; use `rite_calendar` and `rite_calendar_test`.

resource_id.description: Rite-qualified as `<rite>/<calendarId>` for calendar-naming types (e.g. `roman/US`), for `rite_calendar` ids (e.g. `roman/decrees`), and for the `national_calendar_test` and `diocesan_calendar_test` scopes. The deprecated `general_roman_calendar` keeps bare ids such as `decrees` until the #955 prune milestone; `general_roman_calendar_test` and `rite_calendar_test` also stay bare — the latter's id is itself the rite.

review_status.description: This batch's position in the review workflow. Deliberately separate from `publication_status`, which tracks GitHub's side of the same change: an `approved` batch can sit at `publication_status: none` indefinitely in Phase 1, since the publisher that would open a pull request for it does not exist yet.

review_decision.description:
The review outcome AS DECIDED by a human, frozen at the moment of the decision and never rewritten. Null while the batch is still `submitted`, and on a withdrawal.

Read this, not `review_status`, to learn what a reviewer actually decided. The two diverge by design: `markBatchClosedUnmerged()` sets `review_status` to `rejected` when a published pull request is closed without merging — on a batch a human approved — because that is what keeps the batch out of the accumulation base. `review_decision` still reads `approved` for that batch, and `publication_status` explains what became of it.

publication_status.description: This batch's position on GitHub. Phase 1 never writes anything but `none` — `queued`, `open`, `merged` and `closed` are reserved for the Phase 2 publisher and Phase 3 merge polling.

submitted_by_email.description: Null unless the submitter's email was verified at submission time — an unverified email is never recorded here, since it would otherwise become the eventual git commit author.

approved_by_sub.description: OIDC subject of the admin who approved or rejected this batch (the same column serves both decisions). Null while `review_status` is still `submitted`.

rejected_reason.description:
Why this batch stopped. Either the `reason` supplied to POST /admin/change-requests/{batchId}/reject, or text generated by the phase 3 merge poller when a published pull request was closed without merging — so it is NOT exclusively a reviewer's refusal. Pair it with `review_decision` to tell the two apart: `review_decision: "rejected"` means a human wrote this, `review_decision: "approved"` with a `rejected_reason` present means the approval stood and the pull request was later closed.

Null while the batch is still `submitted`, when it was approved and nothing has closed it, when it was withdrawn, and when it was rejected without a reason being given — `reason` on the reject endpoint is optional. Returned to the submitter as well as to reviewers: collecting a human explanation at the moment of refusal and then never showing it to the person it was written for would leave the field write-only.

pr_number.description: GitHub pull request number carrying this batch, stamped by the phase 2 publisher. Null until the batch is published — and also null for a published batch whose pull request could not be resolved, which the publisher counts separately rather than treating as 'not yet published'. This is what lets a history view link to the pull request once one exists.

branch.description: The per-resource branch the phase 2 publisher committed this batch onto. Null until published. Several batches for one resource share a rolling branch and a rolling pull request, so this is not unique per batch.

commit_sha.description: The commit the phase 2 publisher created for this batch. Null until published. Deliberately distinct from each file's `base_sha`, which records what that edit was authored against rather than what it produced.

merge_commit_sha.description: The merge commit GitHub recorded when this batch's pull request merged, stamped by the phase 3 merge poller. Null until then, and permanently null for a batch whose pull request was closed unmerged.

publication_settled_at.description: When this batch's publication reached a terminal state — merged, or closed unmerged — written once by the phase 3 merge poller and never moved again. Null while `publication_status` is `none`, `queued` or `open`. Because it is written exactly once, this is the timestamp a history view should display for a settled batch, rather than `updated_at`, which moves on every later touch.

file_count.description: Number of files in this batch, e.g. 2 for a diocesan calendar plus one i18n translation file.

paths.description: Repository-relative path of every file in this batch, ordered lexicographically under the database collation (not necessarily calendar-file-before-i18n-files).

permissions.description: The OpenFGA `admin` tuple for this batch's resource — mirrors resource_type/resource_id and exists only so the server's own authorization filtering has a uniform shape to check against.

ChangeRequestFile.description: One proposed file inside a change request batch, as returned by the batch detail routes. A batch is a set of file writes submitted together, so reviewing it means reading these.

path.description: Repository-relative path this row proposes to write or delete.

operation.description: What this row does to `path`. Note that `delete` removes THIS FILE, which is not the same as deleting the resource: dropping one locale file from a calendar that still exists is a `delete` too. Whether a batch removes a resource is recorded in the batch's metadata, never inferred from this field.

base_sha.description: Git blob sha of the file this edit was authored against, so a client can tell whether the path has moved underneath the proposal. Null for a row submitted against a path that did not exist yet, and for rows recorded before this column was populated.

content.description: The proposed bytes. Null for a `delete` row, which carries none by table constraint — meaningful data, not missing data. Also null on every row when the request passed `include_content=false`; read `content_included` on the response to tell the two apart.

content_bytes.description: Length in bytes of the proposed content, or null when the row carries none. Always computed from the real content, even when `include_content=false` suppressed the body — which is the point of that switch: a client can size a batch before deciding to fetch it.

current_content.description: The bytes currently at `path` in the deployed source tree, so a client can render a diff rather than a blob. Null when nothing is there (the ordinary case for a `create`), and null on every row when `include_content=false`.

current_content_bytes.description: Length in bytes of what is currently at `path`, or null when nothing is there. Always computed from the real file, even when `include_content=false` suppressed the body.

ChangeRequestBatchDetail.description: One change request batch together with what it actually proposes, returned by GET /admin/change-requests/{batchId} and GET /auth/change-requests/{batchId}. The batch is nested under `batch` rather than spread across the top level so that this schema can reference ChangeRequestBatch — which is additionalProperties: false, and so cannot be extended by an allOf — instead of duplicating every one of its properties. The two routes return an identical body and differ only in who may ask: a reviewer is authorized by the `admin` relation on the batch's resource, a submitter by owning the batch.

files.description: Every row of the batch, ordered by path under the database collation — the same order, and the same paths, as the batch's own `paths` array.

content_included.description: False when the request passed `include_content=false`, meaning every `content` and `current_content` is null because it was suppressed rather than because it is absent. The `content_bytes` and `current_content_bytes` fields stay accurate either way.

ChangeRequestListResponse.description: Offset-paginated page of the caller's own change request batches, returned by GET /auth/change-requests. Scoping is entirely server-side — there is no submitter query parameter, and none will be added, since accepting one would let a caller list someone else's batches. Unlike AdminChangeRequestListResponse, there is no per-caller filtering step after the SQL page is fetched, so there is no `count` or `has_more` here: comparing `offset + <length of change_requests>` against `total` is sufficient to know whether more pages remain.

total.description: Total matching batches for this caller, ignoring limit/offset.

limit.description: Effective limit applied to this page (default 100 if not supplied).

offset.description: Effective offset of the first item in this page (default 0 if not supplied).

AdminChangeRequestListResponse.description: Offset-paginated page of change request batches returned by GET /admin/change-requests. Global admins see every batch, and `count` always equals the SQL page size. Resource (non-global) admins have this page filtered to only the batches whose resource they administer AFTER it is fetched — filtering happens in application code, not SQL, because it depends on OpenFGA relations no query here can express — so for them `count` may be smaller than both `limit` and `total`. `total` always reflects the PRE-filter SQL count, never the post-filter one. `has_more` is likewise derived from the pre-filter SQL page size, never from `count`: clients MUST keep paging on `has_more`, never on whether the current page came back non-empty — a heavily-filtered SQL page can legitimately filter down to zero visible batches while later pages still hold ones the caller can act on.

count.description: Number of items in this page. May be less than `limit`, or than the pre-filter SQL page size, for a resource admin after post-filtering.

total.description: Total matching batches ignoring limit/offset. For resource admins, this is the pre-filter SQL count.

limit.description: Effective limit applied to this page (default 100 if not supplied).

offset.description: Effective offset of the first item in this page (default 0 if not supplied).

has_more.description: True iff more rows are available beyond this page, derived from the PRE-filter SQL paginator state — `(offset + pre-filter SQL page size) < total` — never from the post-filter `count`. See the schema description for why this distinction matters for resource admins.

ChangeRequestDecisionResponse.description: Confirmation returned by POST /admin/change-requests/{batchId}/approve, POST /admin/change-requests/{batchId}/reject, and POST /auth/change-requests/{batchId}/withdraw.

status.description: The batch's review_status after this decision.

PermissionTuple.description: An OpenFGA relationship tuple representing a granted permission

PermissionTupleInput.description: Input for granting or revoking a permission

user.description: Zitadel user ID (with or without 'user:' prefix)

ChangeRequestReviewedNotification.description:
A single review-decision notification item in the authenticated user's inbox: a reviewer approved or REJECTED one of the caller's own submitted source-data change-request batches. One item per batch, not per file.

This is a different event from ChangeRequestNotification, at a different time, and a batch can produce one of each: the decision is when a human judged the proposal, the publication is when GitHub settled it. A rejected batch never publishes at all, so before this type existed a refusal produced no notification of any kind.

Decisions the caller made on their own batch never appear here — the auto-approval a resource admin's own write receives inline is not news, and the write response already answered `disposition: "approved"` synchronously.

One of the shapes UserNotificationsResponse.items may contain. Discriminated on `type`; the shapes share only `type` and `unread`.

review_status.description:
The decision, AS DECIDED. This is the batch's `review_decision`, frozen at the review and never rewritten — deliberately not its current `review_status`, which a later publication failure can move: a published batch whose pull request is closed unmerged is set to `rejected` even though a human approved it. That batch's close is reported separately, as a ChangeRequestNotification with `publication_status: "closed"`.

`approved` does not mean published. An approved batch is queued for publication and settles later; watch for the ChangeRequestNotification carrying the same `batch_id`.

rejected_reason.description: Free-text reason the reviewer gave, when the decision was `rejected` and they supplied one. Null on an approval, and null on a rejection given without a reason. The same value the batch itself reports, so a client may show it inline here rather than fetching the batch.

reviewed_at.description: RFC 3339 UTC timestamp of when the batch was decided. Written once, by the decision itself, and it is the cursor this item is ordered and unread-flagged by — the review-decision counterpart of ChangeRequestNotification.settled_at.

unread.description: True if reviewed_at is more recent than the user's last_seen_at bookmark.

UserNotificationsResponse.description: Response from GET /auth/notifications — the inbox with unread badge metadata. `items` is a discriminated union: clients MUST switch on each item's `type` (`access_request_reviewed`, `change_request_reviewed` or `change_request_published`) before reading any other key — the shapes share only `type` and `unread`. A change-request batch can produce both a `change_request_reviewed` item (when a human decided it) and a `change_request_published` item (when GitHub settled it), carrying the same `batch_id` at different times; a REJECTED batch never publishes and so produces only the former.

RegionalDataLocaleQueryParam.name: locale
RegionalDataLocaleQueryParam.description:
Selects the language of the `name` of every liturgical event in the returned calendar definition, overriding the `Accept-Language` header.

Where the value is read from depends on the method. GET reads it from the query string. POST reads it from the request body instead (see that operation's `requestBody`) and ignores a query string `locale`, because `RegionalDataHandler` merges `getScalarQueryParams()` for GET and `parseBodyParams()` for POST, never both. PUT, PATCH and DELETE accept no `locale` parameter at all: PATCH still resolves one, but only from `Accept-Language`, so a PATCH that sends no such header is negotiated to `la_VA` and refused with `422 Unprocessable Content` by any calendar that does not declare Latin, while PUT and DELETE ignore the locale entirely.

Validation happens in two stages. `RegionalDataParams::setParams()` canonicalises the value and refuses anything that is not a locale this server ships, with `400 Bad Request`. A well-formed locale that the addressed calendar does not itself declare, per the `locales` of its entry on `/calendars`, is then refused with `422 Unprocessable Content`. That second set is data-driven and cannot be enumerated here: `IT` declares only `it_IT`, and the Ambrosian dioceses only `it_IT` and `la_VA`.

This is not the `{i18n_locale}` path segment of `/data/.../{key}/{i18n_locale}`. That segment addresses a different resource, the stored translation map, and binds to a different internal parameter (`i18nRequest`); supplied alongside it, this parameter is still validated, and can still produce the `400` above, but has no effect on the response.

RegionalDataI18nLocalePathParam.name: i18n_locale
RegionalDataI18nLocalePathParam.description:
Names the stored translation file to return, normally one of the locales the addressed calendar declares in its `metadata.locales` (mirrored by `/calendars`). A locale for which the calendar has no file is answered with `404 Not Found` rather than by falling back to another language.

The segment is spelled `i18n_locale` rather than `locale` deliberately. `RegionalDataHandler` binds this third path segment to `i18nRequest`, which selects a different resource, and not to the `locale` parameter that the two-segment `/data` paths accept to choose the language of a calendar definition. The two are independent: a `locale` supplied alongside this segment is still validated, and can still be refused with `400 Bad Request`, but it has no effect on the response.
